content: The document is a detailed and technical report that discusses the systematic reviews of the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive school health services (SHS) in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO). It includes evidence profiles and decision-making frameworks based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. This publication, developed in partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO), provides a systematic review of the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive school health services (SHS). It includes GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks, which are essential tools for evaluating the impact of SHS interventions. The document is part of the WHO guideline on school health services and is publicly available to ensure transparency and accessibility. The publication is licensed under Creative Commons, allowing users to copy, redistribute, and adapt the content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guideline development process involved a global virtual meeting with subgroups from the western and eastern hemispheres. To minimize bias, information from one subgroup was not shared with the other until both had independently evaluated the evidence and made their judgments. Members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) primarily relied on findings from systematic reviews but also incorporated their expertise and knowledge. The systematic reviews included in this publication assess the effectiveness of SHS in achieving critical health outcomes, such as reducing suicide planning, hospitalizations for asthma, emergency department visits for asthma, school absenteeism, and academic progress. For example, one study demonstrated a 43% reduction in emergency department visits for children attending schools with school-based health centers (SBHCs) compared to those without. Another study highlighted improvements in school attendance and academic performance over time for students utilizing SBHCs. The evidence was evaluated using the GRADE methodology, which considers factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, and the quality of the data. For instance, some studies showed significant benefits, but limitations such as small sample sizes or lack of randomization were noted. The publication also emphasizes the importance of addressing the health needs of children and adolescents, as health issues during this critical developmental period can have long-term consequences. The document acknowledges the contributions of various experts, organizations, and funding bodies, including the United Kingdom Department for International Development, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and the United States Agency for International Development. It also includes acknowledgments for the systematic review authors, GDG members, and external reviewers who contributed to the development of the guideline. The publication concludes by reiterating the importance of SHS as a priority for improving the health and education of young people globally. It aligns with international goals and targets, such as those outlined in the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which recognizes the right of every child to the highest attainable standard of health.
